column4: The pilgrimage call brings people on foot and on every lean camel from each distant pass, a direct scene of mounts worn lean by a long road yet reaching its end.

Battle is prosecuted until the enemy is subdued, after which comes release by favor or ransom until war lays down its burdens; warfare, مَنّ in its favor-sense, and the laying down of loads meet in one ayah.
Abu Lahab's wife is named the carrier of firewood, حَمَّالَةَ ٱلْحَطَبِ, a human explicitly characterized by the burden she bears.
A rope of palm fiber is around the load-carrier's neck, joining the carrier in 111:4 to the section's secondary cord image, though here the cord binds rather than supports.
Those who deny meeting God are surprised by the Hour while carrying their burdens on their backs, so denial of judgment becomes a visible load at the journey's end.
Campaigners' thirst, fatigue, hunger, steps that anger the enemy, and gains against him are each written as good work; bodily depletion on the road cannot cut off the wage.
Every expenditure and every valley crossed is recorded for the campaigners so that God may reward their best work, completing the assurance of 9:120.
The patient are paid their reward without reckoning, making endurance answer exhaustion with a wage that has no measured limit.
The command to be patient is followed by the assurance that God does not let the reward of good-doers be lost.
Joseph links taqwa and patience to God's refusal to waste the reward of good-doers, a life-story instance of sustained fidelity receiving its wage.
Those who believe and do righteous works are assured that God does not waste the reward of anyone who perfects work, closely restating the image's unfailed payment.
After the battle and martyrdom passage, the living martyrs rejoice that God does not waste the believers' reward, joining warfare to preserved recompense.
Believers answer God and the Messenger after being wounded; continued response after bodily injury earns a great reward.
Threat of a gathered enemy increases the believers' faith, and they entrust themselves to God instead of losing resolve.
They return with God's favor and bounty, untouched by harm, completing the charge sustained under threat in 3:173.
God will not waste any worker's work, and specifically promises those driven from homes, harmed, fighting, and killed; work, arduous movement, battle, and reward are gathered explicitly.
Those who emigrate after persecution, then strive and remain patient, find the Lord forgiving and merciful; the road continues through trial rather than stopping there.
Creation is ordered to test which people are best in work, giving human عمل a created purpose comparable to the work-fitted animal in the source dictionary.
Earth's adornment is made a test of who is best in work, another direct formulation of created fitness being proved by action.
The question introduces the greatest losers in works, supplying the category whose striving is described as going astray in 18:104.
Humanity is in loss, the broad condition against which reliable work and endurance must prove themselves.
The exception joins belief, good works, truth, and counsel to patience, concentrating the section's reliable side in one formula.
The Prophet is asked whether he demands a wage that leaves the hearers burdened by debt, opposing a humanly crushing fee to the reward supplied by God.
In the same surah that promises the Prophet an uncut wage, the question denies that he asks his hearers for payment that would weigh them down with debt.
A people ask for a king so they may fight, but when fighting is prescribed most turn away, staging a declared charge that fails when performance begins.
Those invited to fight or defend claim they would follow if they knew there would be fighting; their mouths say what their hearts do not contain, joining battlefield withdrawal to unreliable speech.
When fighting is prescribed, a group fears people and asks why the duty was imposed, exposing collapse when the difficult work arrives.
Turning one's back in battle incurs wrath except for a tactical maneuver or regrouping; this supplies the precise boundary to the prohibition in 8:15.
God lightens the believers' battlefield ratio because He knows weakness in them, directly measuring a combat load to present capacity while still requiring patience.
Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask leave from striving with wealth and life, making reliability visible as willing departure.
Those who doubt ask for exemption and waver in uncertainty, the lagging counterpart to the willing campaigners in 9:44.
Some covenant that if God gives bounty they will give charity and become righteous, creating a promise whose reliability is tested by provision.
When bounty arrives they become stingy and turn away, exactly enacting the source dictionary's person who weakens even in generosity.
Hypocrisy follows because they break the promise and lie, connecting failed generosity in 9:76 to كذب as failure to carry through.
Blame falls on people who seek exemption despite being rich enough to go and are content to remain behind, separating chosen lagging from real incapacity.
Under siege, hypocrites call God's and the Messenger's promise a delusion; this false judgment precedes their attempted flight in 33:13.
God identifies those who hinder others and summon them away from battle while scarcely entering the fight themselves.
Their stinginess and terror are exposed together: eyes roll at danger, then sharp tongues demand the good, uniting battlefield collapse with failed generosity.
They wish to be among desert Arabs merely asking for news of the confederates, and even if present would fight little, completing their retreat from the field.
True believers meet the confederates by affirming that God and His Messenger spoke truth, and the danger increases faith and submission rather than breaking the charge.
Those who support God's cause are promised divine support and firm feet, the bodily stability needed by a warrior or traveler who must not falter.
The steadfast fighters beside prophets pray for forgiveness and firm feet, giving the sustaining petition behind the endurance described in 3:146.
God honors the children of Adam by carrying them on land and sea and providing good things, presenting human travel itself as divinely borne.
God enables travel by land and sea; a favorable voyage can suddenly become a storm-bound crisis, a non-animal parallel to transport whose dependable movement fails.
Ships like mountains upon the sea are among God's signs, identifying the great carriers whose motion can be arrested in 42:33.
If God stills the wind, the ships remain motionless on the sea; the halted vehicle is a direct nonlexical counterpart to the mount that can no longer proceed.
Human descendants are carried in the laden ship, ٱلْفُلْكِ ٱلْمَشْحُونِ, extending the image of a burden-bearer from animal to vessel.
God creates comparable things for people to ride, widening the laden ship of 36:41 into a class of provided conveyances.
If God wills, the riders can be drowned with no rescuer, marking the boundary of every created carrier's reliability.
What the stingy withhold will be hung around their necks on Judgment Day, turning failure in generosity into a literal burden.
Jacob questions whether he can trust the brothers again and names God the best guardian, placing reliability inside a dangerous family journey.
Jacob requires a binding pledge that they will bring Benjamin back unless they are overwhelmed, distinguishing broken trust from genuine incapacity on the road.
God commands trusts to be returned to their owners and judgment to be rendered justly, joining the section's reliability root to its closing divine judgment.
The successful believers faithfully guard their trusts and covenants, a concise human form of the source image's reliable bearer.
The same guarding of trusts and covenants recurs among those preserved from anxious instability, reinforcing endurance as reliability over time.
Human creation passes through infancy, maturity, and old age, repeating the arc from developing strength to eventual bodily decline.
Covenants made with God must be fulfilled and confirmed oaths must not be broken, defining reliability as continuation after commitment.
The oath-breaker is likened to a woman who untwists her yarn after it was strong, a direct Quranic reversal from firm cord to failed fibers.
Deceptive oaths can make a foot slip after it was firm and bring punishment for blocking God's path, joining broken trust to a traveler losing footing.
God's covenant must not be exchanged for a small price because what is with God is better, preparing the enduring-versus-exhausted provision stated in 16:96.
Repelling evil with what is better can turn an enemy into a devoted friend, illustrating the good character attributed to the human load-bearer.
Only the patient and greatly favored receive that character, grounding the endurance required for the response in 41:34.
God wills ease rather than hardship in the fast, an explicit boundary ensuring that religious work does not become an incapacitating load.
Ease accompanies hardship, answering the back-breaking burden removed earlier in the surah.
The assurance that ease accompanies hardship is repeated, emphasizing that depletion does not have the final word.
When one task is finished, the Prophet is commanded to exert himself again, making completion the start of renewed work rather than collapse.
Desire is directed toward the Lord, giving the renewed exertion of 94:7 its destination.
The people of the Garden are untouched by fatigue and will never be expelled, reversing both exhaustion and the fear that lasting provision will end.
In the permanent abode, its people say that neither weariness nor fatigue touches them, the clearest final reversal of the spent traveler.
A mother carries her child in weakness upon weakness, making faithful bearing occur through cumulative bodily depletion.
The mother carries and delivers the human with hardship, another literal instance of a burden sustained despite pain.
In the duties of nursing, no soul is charged beyond capacity and neither parent is to be harmed through the child; a concrete family load is measured to strength.
The command to protect an orphan's property and give full measure is bounded by charging no soul beyond capacity, bringing just work under a measured load.
People are told to obey and spend as far as able, and those protected from their own stinginess succeed; capacity and generosity are treated together.
The Helpers prefer others despite their own need, and safety from inner stinginess marks success, directly reversing weakness in generosity.
The God-conscious spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people, combining durable generosity with the good character named in the source dictionary.
The hypocrites approach prayer lazily and spend only unwillingly, pairing drained worship with failed generosity.
The secure sanctuary receives fruits as provision, joining safety with dependable supply at the journey's destination.
God makes a sanctuary secure while people around it are snatched away, defining the protected boundary implied by the trusted place and mount.
The believers are promised entry into the Sacred Mosque in safety, making security the realized endpoint of their interrupted pilgrimage journey.
The righteous are told to enter the Garden in peace and safety, carrying the security word to the final dwelling where fatigue is absent.
The God-conscious are in a secure station, مَقَامٍ أَمِينٍ, an enduring destination that reverses the unsafe, exhausting road.
The believers did not spur horse or camel to obtain this property; the ayah marks a boundary where provision comes without the mounted military exertion central to the image.
Sacrificial camels stand in rows, then fall on their sides and feed both contented and needy people; the animal's strength, fall, and conversion into provision form a distinct camel scene.
The frustrated opponent is told to extend a cord and then cut it; this may echo the section's weak-cord and severance details, though the ayah's difficult image is not a load rope.

A traveler passing a ruined town is stopped by death for a century while his donkey becomes part of the resurrection sign; the halted journey and mount are specific, but the stop is miraculous rather than exhaustion.
The unjust person lies about God and denies truth when it arrives, presenting unreliability as rejection of the true message.
The one who brings truth and confirms it is God-conscious, the direct reliable counterpart to the liar in 39:32.
Those truthful people have whatever they wish with their Lord, beginning the reward for reliability identified in 39:33.
God covers their worst deeds and pays them for their best, completing the sequence from truthful response to preserved wage.
People prefer the nearer life, choosing the immediate stage of the journey over its lasting outcome.
The Hereafter is better and more enduring, directly opposing transient strength and provision with what remains.
